notes.25:1: The Clementine Vulgate adds 'and the bride' (et sponsae), a reading supported by several Old Latin and Syriac witnesses but absent from standard Greek editions.
notes.25:15: The Vulgate places 'immediately' (statim) at the end of v. 15 modifying the master's departure, whereas many modern Greek editions attach the adverb to the first servant's departure at the start of v. 16.
notes.25:29: The Clementine Vulgate reads 'even what he seems to have' (et quod videtur habere, paralleling Luke 8:18), whereas standard Greek manuscripts of Matthew read simply 'even what he has.'
notes.25:31: The Vulgate translates Greek doxa ('glory') as majestas ('majesty') in both occurrences here, and Greek thronos as sedes ('seat' or 'throne').
notes.25:40: Here and in v. 45, the Vulgate translates Greek eph' hoson ('to the extent that') temporally as quamdiu ('as long as'); note also the Vulgate shift from superlative 'least brothers of Mine' (fratribus meis minimis) in v. 40 to comparative 'these lesser ones' (minoribus his) in v. 45.
notes.26:15: The Vulgate uses constituerunt ("assigned," "appointed," or "set"), emphasizing the fixing of an agreed payment rather than physically weighing out the silver.
notes.26:20: The Clementine Vulgate explicitly reads cum duodecim discipulis suis ("with His twelve disciples"), where critical Greek texts read simply "with the twelve."
notes.26:28: The Clementine Vulgate retains novi ("new") in novi testamenti ("of the new covenant") and uses the future passive effundetur ("will be poured out"), whereas critical Greek editions omit "new" and use a present participle.
notes.26:31: The Vulgate translates the Greek passive verb periphrastically as scandalum patiemini ("will suffer stumbling" or "scandal"), distinguishing it from the passive verb forms of scandalizo in 26:33.
notes.26:50: The Vulgate renders the elliptical Greek clause eph' ho parei as a direct question, ad quid venisti? ("for what purpose have you come?").
notes.26:61: The Clementine Vulgate reads post triduum ("after three days") and reaedificare ("rebuild"), whereas the Greek reads dia trion hemeron ("within three days") and oikodomesai ("build").
notes.26:62: The Vulgate combines the high priest's words into a single question (Nihil respondes ad ea, quae isti adversum te testificantur?), whereas the Greek divides them into two separate questions.
notes.26:64: The Clementine Vulgate explicitly includes Dei ("of God") in virtutis Dei ("of the power of God") and uses in ("in the clouds of heaven"), whereas critical Greek texts read simply "of Power" and "on the clouds of heaven."
notes.27:4: The Vulgate reads sanguinem justum ("righteous blood"), whereas critical Greek editions read "innocent blood"; the Vulgate likewise includes justi ("righteous") in v. 24, which modern critical Greek texts omit.
notes.27:8: The Vulgate distinctively includes Haceldama, hoc est ("Akeldama, that is"), a reading absent from the Greek text of Matthew 27:8 and parallel to Acts 1:19.
notes.27:16: The Vulgate uses the singular verb habebat ("he had," referring to Pilate the governor), whereas the Greek text has the plural ("they had").
notes.27:33: Latin Calvariae locus literally means "Place of a Skull" (calvaria = skull), translating Aramaic Golgotha; this Latin term is the origin of the traditional English name "Calvary."
notes.27:35: The fulfillment quotation ("so that what was spoken... they cast lots," citing Psalm 22:18 / Vulg. 21:19) is present in the Clementine Vulgate (parallel to John 19:24) but absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and modern critical Greek editions of Matthew.
notes.27:40: The Vulgate includes both the scornful interjection Vah! ("Aha!", parallel to Mark 15:29) and Dei ("of God") after templum, neither of which appears in modern critical Greek editions of Matthew 27:40.
notes.27:42: The Vulgate reads si ("if") before rex Israel est and uses the present indicative credimus ("we believe"), whereas critical Greek editions omit "if" and read the future ("we will believe").
notes.28:1: The Vulgate reads Vespere ("in the evening") for the close of the Sabbath day, followed by feminine quæ and prima sabbati (literally "first of the Sabbath," an idiom for the first day of the week) with "day" or "hour" implied.
notes.28:3: Unlike Greek manuscripts that describe the angel's garment as "white as snow," the Clementine Vulgate reads simply sicut nix ("like snow").
notes.28:6: The Clementine Vulgate reads ubi positus erat Dominus ("where the Lord had been laid"), using a pluperfect passive verb and explicitly naming "the Lord" where critical Greek texts read simply "where he lay."
notes.28:7: The Clementine Vulgate reads simply quia surrexit ("that He has risen"), without the phrase "from the dead" present in Greek manuscripts, and uses prædixi ("I have told you beforehand") at the close of the angel's speech.
notes.28:19: The Vulgate renders the command as docete omnes gentes ("teach all nations") rather than "make disciples of all nations" (the sense of the Greek verb), and uses in nomine ("in the name of") with the ablative case.

unplaced.text: For the Son of Man came to save what had been lost.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you devour the houses of widows while praying long prayers! For this reason you will receive a greater judgment.
unplaced.note: The Clementine Vulgate reads "orationes longas orantes" ("praying long prayers") without any phrase equivalent to "for a pretense."
